job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Aaron Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aaron, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in a flat in Westbrook. My dad drives a taxi and my mum works as a home health aide, so we're always counting. Most days I put on a shirt, sit at the kitchen table and apply to banks, insurers and building societies, because that's what my degree is for. In the afternoon I walk to the library, and in the evening I help my dad with the taxi accounts, which he keeps in a notebook.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what has the search been like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a bachelor's in finance at Westbrook University and passed with an average mark. My final project was a comparison of savings accounts for first-time customers, and my tutor said it was tidy but nothing special. I had no internship because I worked evenings at my uncle's electronics shop. In eight months I've sent about fifty applications, mostly online forms, and heard back from five with automatic rejections. I owe a heavy loan and have about three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds about right. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything, and then it's a better calculator. I wouldn't say much at all, to be honest, and I wouldn't post anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means my situation stays the same, which is not good. There are very few finance jobs in Westbrook, and each posting has hundreds of applicants. I'd be glad if things stayed steady, but steady for me is still no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to banks, insurers and the building society, around ten a week, and I'd add the council finance office. I'd ask my uncle for more hours at the electronics shop, since it pays something. I'd keep helping my dad with the taxi books, and maybe get him a proper spreadsheet, although he'd resist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired and a bit embarrassed, honestly. When relatives ask what I'm doing, I say I'm applying, which sounds like nothing. I don't feel panic, just a low weight I carry around all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you only apply to banks and insurers. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what the course taught, and I know how those places work. A bank has a clear ladder, a graduate scheme, a training plan. A start-up or a tech firm feels like a gamble, and I can't afford one. I'd rather wait for a proper offer than jump into something with no structure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like a job, any job with a pay slip, even if it's not perfect. I'd like to start paying my parents something towards the flat. And I'd like to stop feeling like a burden at dinner. That's all, really.

say: I'd say AI is **probably a better calculator**, and I'd keep my views mostly to myself.
think: My situation stays the same, and **steady** for me still means no job.
Westbrook has very few finance jobs, and each posting gets hundreds of applicants.
do: Send around ten applications a week to banks, insurers and the building society.
Ask my uncle for **more hours** at the electronics shop.
Help my dad turn his taxi notebook into a simple spreadsheet.
feel: Tired and a bit embarrassed, carrying a **low weight** all day.
S0.quote: I'd rather wait for a proper offer than jump into something with no structure.
fieldNote: Prefers **structure**: graduate schemes and clear ladders over risky firms.
His worry is quiet and constant, not dramatic.
Applies only where he knows how the system works, which narrows his options.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to banks and insurers
Apply to the council finance office as well
Ask my uncle for extra hours at the electronics shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to wait and see how it works out, since nobody really knows. I'd listen to what the bank bosses say about hiring. I'd probably tell my dad that his taxi books could be done by an app, and he'd laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. Banks are exactly the kind of place where checking, planning and customer chat get taken over by software. The graduate schemes are probably the first to shrink, and they were my whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to places that need a person to carry responsibility, like building societies, local credit unions and small accounting firms. I'd still avoid learning AI tools on my own, I'll admit, because I'm slow with new software and I don't trust it. But I'd probably sit through a course if a firm offered one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit let down. I've done everything the right way and the road might close. It's like studying for a train that's being taken off the timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Banks are full of the tasks the card names. How do you think that affects the graduate schemes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer places, higher bars. A bank that hires thirty graduates now might hire ten, and ask for coding or data skills I don't have. My course had one module on spreadsheets and nothing on that. I'd be behind the people who learned it for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to tell you which jobs are safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My tutor, I think, and maybe an older person in the building society who's seen changes before. I wouldn't trust news headlines or the firms selling the tools. I'd want someone who has nothing to sell.

I'd listen to what the bank bosses say about hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and banks should slow down and talk to people before doing anything, because two years is not enough. I wouldn't shout, but I'd sign a petition. I'd tell my dad we need to talk about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my degree is worth nothing, and I'd feel foolish for having borrowed so much for it. I'd think of my parents, who worked for decades, and now their son is stuck. I wouldn't know what else I'm good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit with my parents and put all our costs on paper. I'd tell my uncle I want every shift available at the shop, and I'd ask my dad whether I could drive a few evenings on his licence if the rules allow. I'd also ask the council about hardship support. I'd stay away from new training, because I couldn't pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like a wet coat. I'd be ashamed, too, because I'd have nothing to offer them. I'd go to bed early to avoid thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first thing you did in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, because the taxi is the only income that isn't already shaky. Self-driving cars would be next, but that's after 2031, so he has a few years. My mum's job is hands-on, so it should last. My lack of income would be the biggest hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your house would be hit hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my laptop only as a last resort, I need it for applications. I'd cut my phone plan to the cheapest, stop the library bus pass and walk. And I'd ask the loan company about deferral, although I'm nervous about that phone call.

say: I'd say governments and banks should **slow down** and talk to people first.
I'd sign a petition, but I wouldn't shout.
think: My degree would be worth nothing, and I'd feel **foolish** for borrowing so much.
I wouldn't know what else I'm good for.
do: Put all household costs on paper with my parents in the **first month**.
Ask my uncle for every shift at the electronics shop.
Call the loan company about **deferral** and the council about hardship support.
feel: Heavy, like a **wet coat**, with shame about having nothing to offer my parents.
S2.quote: I'd think of my parents, who worked for decades, and now their son is stuck.
fieldNote: Shame and **family duty** drive his answers more than anger.
Plans are small and practical, avoiding new training he can't pay for.

steps.text: Write down every household cost with my parents

Phone the loan company about a deferral
Sign a petition for slower rollout and worker support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that people should make some sensible rules. I'd say it quietly to my relatives and tell my dad to learn some of the tools too. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels more manageable. If I get a job in the next year or two, I'd have a few years to build up some savings and a reason to be kept on. I'd be twenty-eight by 2031, which is not old, but I'd need to be doing something that isn't just numbers on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any steady job, even in an admin office at a firm that makes things, and stay there. I'd save fifty pounds a month, pay my parents rent, and take evening classes in something practical like payroll or tax law. I'd also try one of those AI tools at last, with my cousin sitting next to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a thread of hope. I'd feel there's a chance to do things in the right order, instead of everything at once. It's still a hard picture because I'm not good at changing quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm slow with new things, I know that. But five years is long enough to learn it at my own speed, if someone shows me properly. I'd start with one tool and a simple job, like summarising a long document, and see if I get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid AI tools with five years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a trade-like skill in money or admin, something with a licence or a stamp. Those are the things that hold longer. I'd say don't gamble on being first at anything.

I'd say it quietly to relatives.
think: It feels more **manageable**: with a job soon I'd have years to save and a reason to be kept.
I'd need to be doing something that isn't just numbers on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to sort themselves out, and I'd not worry too much in public. I'd say the same to friends who are anxious: take it step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I'm not in a race. Ten years is long enough to do an apprenticeship in finance, to get a qualification and settle down. I'd be thirty-three, maybe married, maybe with a flat. The only trouble is getting that first job soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job to start, then do part-time study for an accounting qualification. I'd save a hundred pounds a month, pay down the loan and help my parents with the rent. I'd start using AI tools slowly once they're standard where I work, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than with the other pictures, though not carefree. I still don't have a job today, and ten years starts from now. I'd feel there's time to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what does a good outcome look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job in a firm, a pay slip, a small flat with a bit of garden, and being able to pay for my parents' holiday once. That's a good outcome. Nothing fancy, just stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say learn a skill nobody can take away, and he'd say it in about four words. He's seen the taxi trade change with apps, and he says you can't fight it, you can only keep driving. I'd listen to him more than any expert.

I'd tell anxious friends to take it step by step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because there'd be no time to change and my parents have no cushion. What would help is a loan deferral, a clear path into some job and being told honestly where the work is going. Even a mentor would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that quiet people like me exist. We aren't shouting about anything, but we're worried, and we'd take a plain, ordinary job if anyone offered one.

headlineQuote: We aren't shouting about anything, but we're worried, and we'd take a plain, ordinary job if anyone offered one.
portrait: Aaron (23) lives with his parents in a flat in **Westbrook**, owes a heavy loan and has about three weeks of savings.
He holds a pass in finance with no internship and has had five automatic rejections from fifty applications.
He is quiet, wants **structure** and doesn't use AI tools, preferring to learn slowly.
He trusts his father and tutor more than experts, and shame about being a burden shows in many answers.
He grows calmer only when there is a decade to find a **steady job**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because there'd be no time and his parents have no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan deferral**, a clear path into any job and honest word on where work is going.
